newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan polls present various scenarios for markets.
newsitem.headline: Japan polls present various scenarios for markets.

text.p: The announcement on Friday of a Japanese general election date caused little reaction in Tokyo markets, but analysts said they may need to rethink strategies depending on the outcome of the October 20 poll.
While many dealers said it was too early to trade on the possible effect of the election, analysts said there were numerous post-poll scenarios.

"The dissolution of parliament itself had no impact. If there were to be any, it would depend on the structure of the next government," said Koji Asano, senior manager of foreign exchange at Fuji Bank.
Friday's dissolution of parliament and the October 20 election date had been an open secret for weeks.
In the unlikely event that Shinshinto, the main opposition, were to win a majority, interest rates could soar considerably, said Yasunari Ueno, chief market economist at Fuji Securities.
Shinshinto (New Frontier Party) is calling for a freezing of the government's plan to raise the consumption tax to five percent from the current three percent next April.
Although recent polls have suggested that the odds of a Shinshinto win are not high, its policy, if implemented, would put upward pressure on interest rates in two ways, Ueno said.

First, he said, the economy would be more likely to pick up if the consumption tax rate were left intact as consumption was likely to suffer from the tax increase. Secondly, a government wishing to keep the tax rate down would need to make up for revenue shortfalls by new bond issues that would push up interest rates.
Fuji Bank's Asano said any moves in Japanese interest rates would affect the foreign exchange market.
"What matters for the forex market now is the interest-rate picture," he said.
Ueno said that if the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) -- currently by far the strongest party which headed the outgoing ruling coalition -- wins a majority of seats, interest rates would head down.
Historically, a stable Japanese government has favoured a strong yen, which would mean lower interest rates, he said.

Taisuke Tanaka, a strategist at Credit Suisse, argued that a powerful LDP government might feel itself obliged to implement a large supplementary budget to stimulate the economy, given its ties to various business groups.
This would require more bonds issues, which would in turn push up interest rates.
The latest opinion polls have predicted a far less clear-cut scenario than an overall majority for any party, however.
Political analysts say the LDP is likely to remain the dominant party but to fall short of a simple majority, forcing it to forge a coalition with a smaller party.
The newly built reformist Democratic Party could claim a fairly large number of seats and become the second party in a coalition with the all-important casting vote.
Many analysts see a coalition between the LDP and the Democrats as the most likely choice.

Asano said a coalition government with the LDP at its core would have little impact on markets, but Ueno said that coalitions were often often unstable and inherently cautious about policy, and such a scenario could lead to yen selling.
Tanaka of Credit Suisse said there could be splits and realignments in and among the parties even after the election should no party win a simple majority.
For instance, he said, Shinshinto could split and a faction form a conservative government with the LDP.
"At the moment, I can only say there are many conceivable scenarios," he said.
